articles.title: Dust Extraction System
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Somewhere in a workshop, there’s a dust extractor already plugged in and switched on. It prevents the debris from going up in the air. This makes the job of an air scrubber or air purifier a lot easier. However, its effectiveness comes down to a handful of practical decisions. Owning one just won’t cut it. Match Extraction Power to the Tools Being Used A shop vac or basic extractor pulls a fraction of the airflow that a properly sized system delivers, and airflow is what captures dust at the source. articles.title: Life After Trump
articles.author: Dick Price, Ken Levy
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The pre-Trump world is gone. But what replaces it? That was the central question posed by Ken Levy, LMFT, during his October 3 presentation, Life After Trump , at the 4th Annual Left Coast Forum at Cal State LA. Levy, a community-focused psychotherapist, longtime activist, and Coordinating Committee member of the Northeast LA Alliance for Democracy, challenged participants to look beyond the daily turbulence of the Trump presidency and confront a more fundamental problem: America cannot simply return to the political arrangements that made Trumpism possible. articles.title: Neukölln, the Berlin District Where the Left Broke Through
articles.author: Frederik Blauwhof
articles.content_excerpt: Amid resounding recent victories for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), on September 20 Germany’s socialist party Die Linke bucked the trend with a spectacular victory in Berlin. It dominated the campaign with its program of ending cuts, capping rents, and socializing housing companies, leaving other parties to respond to the popular demand that Berliners had confirmed in a 2021 referendum . The monster victory for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt further galvanized Berlin’s diverse urban working class to express opposition to the fascists. Die Linke’s doubling of its vote in Berlin, winning 25.7 percent support, was no blip. articles.author: LM Jackson
articles.content_excerpt: It's been an arduous day in the prison laundry, where I have spent the last four hours loading and unloading the three industrial-size dryers under my care. The one-ounce scoop of peanut butter served with two pieces of white bread and a one-ounce serving of canned fruit I received at breakfast failed to provide me with sufficient calories for the energy required to complete my task. articles.title: A Portrait of Eugene Debs for Today’s Left
articles.author: Matthew E. Stanley
articles.content_excerpt: You can tell the capitalist system is in trouble when Americans start talking about Eugene Debs. Although the popular image of the great labor and socialist leader has ebbed and flowed since his death a century ago this month, our New Gilded Age has placed him back in the spotlight. Progressive politicians and labor activists, including United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain and union organizer Jaz Brisack, quote his speeches with regularity. Last year, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez traveled to Debs’s home in Terre Haute, Indiana, to introduce Bernie Sanders, who has long cited the Hoosier firebrand as a political hero. In these last weeks before the midterms, Democratic candidates have been gaining ground by talking about two things: the affordability crisis and political corruption. If Democrats regain control of Congress and genuinely want to respond to affordability, they’ll need to do everything possible to root out the corruption. The two are inseparable. In large part, prices are rising faster than paychecks because so much of the economy has become subject to political bribery, Trump Republican pay-to-play schemes, and kickbacks to Trump and his cronies. 1. articles.title: Gen Z Protests Are Reshaping Asia
articles.author: Ruhi Bhasin
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Asia has seen a surge of “Gen Z protests,” led by a generation tired of accepting the status quo and increasingly using social media to drive change in deeply entrenched political systems. In India, protests over the education system helped force the education minister’s resignation in 2026. Protests in Bangladesh and Nepal in 2024 and 2025, respectively, led to government changes. These protests have helped expose fractured political structures in these countries. Governments in several South and Southeast Asian countries have done little to address the economic distress and corruption plaguing them. Only recently, after a mere two decades of intermittent conflict (with three years off ), the last U.S. troops finally withdrew from... yes, can you believe it?... Iraq! Don’t be shocked, since we’re talking about a country significantly less than 7,000 miles from our shores. articles.title: In Russia’s Election, Nothing Happened, but Things Got Worse
articles.author: Maria Chiara Franceschelli
articles.content_excerpt: Between September 18 and 20, Russians voted for a new State Duma, along with several regional parliaments and governors. According to the Central Election Commission, turnout reached 59.8 percent, up eight points since 2021. The result was the one everyone expected. Vladimir Putin’s United Russia took almost 58 percent of the party-list vote and 349 of the Duma’s 450 seats, up from 310 in the outgoing chamber. Forty-one of its new MPs are veterans of the invasion of Ukraine. The Communist Party (KPRF) came a distant second with thirty-seven seats, followed by the Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR) with twenty-three, New People with nineteen, A Just Russia with seventeen, and Rodina with one. articles.title: The Impossible Will Take a Little While: The Power of Persistence
articles.author: Paul Rogat Loeb
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. We live in a time fraught with bad news: assaults on democracy, climate disasters, crippling inequality, and an endless proliferation of lies. The pace of the daily outrages reminds me of a moment from Art Spiegelman’s Maus . The Spiegelman character asks his therapist, a concentration camp survivor, what it felt like to be in the camps. His therapist thinks, and then yells “Boo!” as loudly as he can, and Spiegelman jumps back. “It felt a little like that,” his therapist says. “But always! articles.title: All Aboard Eugene Debs’s Red Special
articles.author: Shawn Gude
articles.content_excerpt: The specially chartered locomotive pulled out of Chicago on a late August day in 1908, heading west, a sleeper car, dining car, and baggage car loaded with socialist pamphlets in tow. Red flags poked out, bunting and streamers festooning the sides. The passengers were in high spirits. Socialist Party presidential candidate Eugene V. articles.author: Sharon Kyle, Dick Price
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Alexander Hamilton famously described the judiciary as the “least dangerous” branch of government. Unlike Congress, it controlled no purse. Unlike the president, it commanded no army. Its principal power was judgment. More than two centuries later, that description is being put to the test. In a special Left Coast Forum discussion presented by LA Progressive, USC law professor Jody Armour joined constitutional scholars Marjorie Cohn and Stephen Rohde to examine a much larger question than whether the current Supreme Court is conservative: Is the Roberts Court fundamentally changing the constitutional balance of power? articles.title: UAW President Shawn Fain Wins Mandate in Reelection Victory
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content_excerpt: Kentucky Auto Workers joined the crowd in Detroit for the rally that kicked off the Stand-Up Strike September 15. Photo: Jim West, jimwestphoto.com . By Luis Feliz Leon and Jane Slaughter United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain has won a second four-year term, with an overwhelming lead in member balloting for the union’s top officers. The election was a referendum on the new fighting direction Fain has taken the union by leading 2023’s Stand-Up Strike against the Big 3 automakers, other bold contract fights, and new organizing campaigns. It marks the second time members have voted for their top officers in the union’s 91 years. UAW members voted to switch to a one-member-one-vote system in December 2021.
